subject: PacketWorks: packetized streaming emit & first-token SLA tradeoffs
messages:
From: Priya Natarajan <priya_natarajan@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Chen <alex.chen@packetworks.io>, DevOps POC <ops@packetworks.io>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-07-18T15:12:00-07:00
Subject: PacketWorks discovery recap — first-token targets & pilot asks

Alex / Team,

Thanks again for taking time today — helpful session. Quick recap of the performance items we discussed and proposed next steps so internal folks and your ops team are aligned. I kept it intentionally tight.

Key goals you called out on the call:
- TTFT (time-to-first-token): target P50 under 200ms, P95 under 700ms for your main inference path when under normal peak (expected baseline traffic).
- Sustained concurrency: design for 150–250 concurrent active streams (mostly short responses, 60–200 tokens).
- Preferred streaming mode: SSE for one-way streaming from model to client; open to WebSocket if you need bi-directional control/cancellation.
- Chunk cadence: aim for initial chunk within ~200ms of request; subsequent chunks every 100–250ms depending on payload shape (you said many responses are concise).

Pilot asks (what we'd like from PacketWorks to validate these SLAs):
1) Sample payloads: 200 representative messages (mix of short/medium/long, avg length + 90th percentile lengths).
2) Traffic profile: expected RPS and concurrency during a typical 1-hour peak window and a stress window (95th/99th).
3) Access: temporary API keys and Env details for us to run a controlled soak and ramp test (we will provide an IP allowlist).
4) Success criteria: TTFT P50 <200ms, P95 <700ms, and drop/failure rate <0.5% during a 1-hour 100 RPS soak with concurrency ramp to target.

Notes on tradeoffs we flagged on the call:
- SSE vs WebSocket: SSE is simpler to integrate for uni-directional streams and has slightly better scaling for short-lived connections in many proxies; WebSocket is better if you need cancellation, client-side feedback, or multi-turn auth flows.
- Chunk cadence vs throughput: smaller, more frequent chunks reduce perceived latency but increase overhead on the runtime and network. For you, a cadence around 120–180 tokens per chunk (or 100–200ms cadence) is a reasonable starting point.

Next steps: can you share the sample payload set and the traffic profile by end of day Tuesday (2027-07-20)? Once we have that, Ben and I will propose a pilot configuration and a lightweight test plan.

Attachments: packetworks_mop_v1.pdf (pilot mapping doc stub)

Best,
Priya Natarajan

From: Alex Chen <alex.chen@packetworks.io>

Cc: DevOps POC <ops@packetworks.io>
Date: 2027-07-19T09:44:00-07:00
Subject: Re: PacketWorks discovery recap — first-token targets & pilot asks

Thanks Priya — that matches our notes. A few clarifications from our side: 

1) Traffic profile: typical peak is ~80 RPS, burst up to 220 RPS for short periods (5–10 minutes). Concurrency tends to be higher because many clients hold open the SSE stream while waiting for additional context.
2) Payload mix: about 60% short responses (<= 80 tokens), 30% medium (80–250 tokens), 10% long (>250 tokens).
3) Cancellation: we do occasionally cancel streams from the client side when users navigate away — that argues for WebSocket in a small subset, but SSE could be fine if we implement a heartbeat and early-abort semantics at the proxy.

We can assemble the sample payloads and a short CSV with the traffic histograms. Ops can stand up a temporary endpoint and provide an allowlist for Redwood IPs. Will aim to have that to you by EOD 20-Jul.

Quick question: do you need the 1-hour soak to be at our peak (220 RPS) or at the sustained 100 RPS you referenced? We want to make sure we allocate the right infra.

— Alex

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>

Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-07-20T11:03:00-07:00
Subject: RE: PacketWorks discovery recap — pilot config suggestions

Alex / Priya — looped in a couple of recommended pilot configurations and what we'll measure. High-level notes below; I'll attach a short SLO spreadsheet (slo-proposal.xlsx) with the exact measurement buckets.

Pilot config options (start with option A, escalate to B if you want harder numbers):
A) Functional pilot (low-cost, fast):
- Run 1-hour soak at 100 RPS, concurrency ramp from 50 to 150.
- Model: our production candidate (8-bit quantized) with SSE.
- Chunking: initial 1st-chunk target = under 200ms; subsequent chunks every ~150ms or ~120 tokens (whichever fires first).
- Metrics: TTFT P50/P95, payload throughput, connection churn, and error/drop rate.

B) Stress pilot (deeper):
- 2-hour soak with bursts to 220 RPS for 5min every 15min. Concurrency target up to 250.
- Also test WebSocket path for cancellation behavior and measure connection overhead.

Operational tradeoffs I want to highlight:
- Pushing for P95 < 300–400ms will likely require more expensive reserved capacity and tuned batching. If PacketWorks is comfortable with P95 <700ms initially, we can iterate on optimizations that improve cost/P95 tradeoffs.
- Chunk frequency: smaller chunks (under 100 tokens) increase request rate to the runtime and can amplify queuing under load. The ~120-token / 150ms cadence is often a pragmatic balance.

We will provide a test harness and scripts and can run the tests in your staging environment. Let us know which pilot option you prefer and whether you want the WebSocket path included.

Attachments: slo-proposal.xlsx

Cheers,
Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference
ben_carter@redwood.ai

Subject: PacketWorks pilot plan & ask for artifacts (confirming option A)

Alex — thanks for the quick reply and for assembling the payloads. Sounds like a plan. For speed, PacketWorks and Redwood should start with Pilot Option A (1-hour soak at 100 RPS, concurrency ramp 50->150) so we can validate TTFT behavior without committing to heavy infra. If Option A looks healthy, we'll schedule the stress pilot B the following week.

Action items and owners:
- PacketWorks (Alex / Ops): share sample payloads (200 items) + traffic CSV + staging endpoint and allowlist by EOD 2027-07-20 — status: pending (you indicated this will be ready).
- Redwood (Ben): finalize the slo-proposal.xlsx thresholds and test harness by EOD 2027-07-20 — status: in progress (attached).
- Redwood (Priya): set up a 60-minute pilot window on Fri 2027-07-23 and share the runbook link + DocuSign access for a temporary pilot agreement.

Acceptance criteria reminder: TTFT P50 <200ms and P95 <700ms on the pilot run; connection drop rate <0.5%. If we meet those, we'll move to stress pilot B and discuss cost/commitment tradeoffs (reserved capacity options).

I'll post the pilot runbook to the shared Drive and send the calendar invite once we have confirmation on the staging endpoint. Looking forward to running this.
